oneliner.t: Republican state representative from Enterprise (House District 91 since 2018) and former tire-and-auto business owner, endorsed by Trump, who won the Aug. 11, 2026 AL-02 special primary after his home was redrawn out of AL-01.

born.note: Birthplace in Wikipedia and Ballotpedia. Birth date from Wikipedia only.

upbringing.t: Raised in Spanish Fort in Baldwin County. Graduated from Fairhope High School in 1990 and earned a marketing degree from the University of Alabama in 1994. He says close family still lives in Baldwin County and that he raised his daughters in Coffee County, where he owned Goodson Tire & Auto in Enterprise. He later sold the business and has been an employee of Jim Whaley Tires, Inc. since 2023.

career.role: State Representative, House District 91 (member, House Health Committee)

platform.t: Pledges to support President Trump's agenda and reverse 'four years of failed Biden economic policies.'
July 2026 ad: will work with Trump to deport criminal illegal immigrants, ban DEI, and 'keep boys out of girls' locker rooms.'
Cites state-level record on grocery tax cuts, the diaper/baby-supply tax exemption and senior tax relief.
Touts his votes for Alabama's near-total abortion ban and a 2026 law extending the death penalty to child sexual assault.
Supports the war with Iran to stop Iran from getting nuclear weapons. The DCCC says he called the resulting cost increases a 'temporary setback.'

promises.t: Work with Trump to deport criminal illegal immigrants, ban DEI, and keep boys out of girls' locker rooms.
Help keep a Republican House majority.
Unify the district 'from the peanut fields to the beaches' (said while running in AL-01).

claims.claim: Born and raised in Baldwin County.
claims.short: Born and raised in Baldwin County

record.t: Born in Spanish Fort, Baldwin County; Fairhope High School 1990. One Reflector article (Aug 13, 2026) calls him a 'native of Coffee County', which conflicts with these sources.

claims.claim: Has served two terms in the Alabama Legislature.

record.t: Elected HD-91 in 2018 and re-elected in 2022.

claims.claim: Small business owner who built his business in the Wiregrass, creating jobs.

record.t: Owned and managed Goodson Tire & Auto in Enterprise (Coffee County). He has since sold it and has been an employee of Jim Whaley Tires since 2023, so 'business owner' is past tense. Job numbers not documented.

claims.claim: Worked in the Legislature to cut state taxes on groceries.

record.t: The 2023 law cut the 4% state grocery tax to 3% (and to 2% in 2024 if revenue triggers were met). The House gave final passage 103–0 on June 1, 2023. His individual roll-call vote was not opened; he was not reported as a sponsor.

claims.claim: Worked in the Alabama Legislature to eliminate the state tax on diapers and baby supplies.

record.t: HB152 (2025) exempts diapers, baby formula and related items from the state sales tax only, from Sep 1, 2025 through Aug 31, 2028 (temporary). Sponsor was Rep. Neil Rafferty (D) with co-sponsors not including Marques. The House passed it unanimously. Overstates his role and the permanence.

claims.claim: Passed a tax relief package for seniors.

record.t: Listed as a House sponsor of HB162 (2022), which exempts the first $6,000 of retirement income for people 65+ starting tax year 2023.

claims.claim: The 'America First fighter President Trump trusts.'

record.t: Trump endorsed Marques in June 2026 (checkable part only; 'fighter' is opinion).

claims.claim: Voted for Alabama's near-total abortion ban.

record.t: He was a House member when the 2019 ban passed, but the roll call was not opened here.

entries.t: Voted for the Rebuild Alabama fuel-tax increase (al.com via Wikipedia). GOP primary rivals criticized it in 2026.
When rival David Matthews cited 22 House votes for tax increases, Marques said they were local bills for other counties.

aipac_endorse.t: Not checked — AIPAC's endorsement page is not on this environment's allowed source list.

aipac_pac.note: Not listed on Track AIPAC's Congress or Candidates pages as of Oct 8, 2026.

fec.src_note: pac_all = FEC 'other committee contributions' (split not available). Itemized individual money is 85% of receipts. His FEC ID carries an AL01 prefix because he first registered in District 1.
fec.quarters_note: Rounded 'more than' figures from Alabama Daily News. The Q3-25 figure is the campaign's own announcement.
fec.outside_note: No independent expenditures for or against Marques found in news coverage. The NRCC named AL-02 a priority, but no dollar figures were reported. FEC outside-spending tables were not reachable.
fec.history_note: Only federal race. State House races (2018: $118,526 raised; 2022: $160,002 per Ballotpedia, sourced from OpenSecrets/FEC) were filed with the Alabama FCPA, which is blocked.

money_flags_note: Not a clean finding. $188,468.70 in PAC/committee money (FEC) could not be itemized by contributor, so business-PAC money cannot be confirmed or ruled out. Known committee donors are candidate and leadership committees (Sen. Katie Britt's campaign $6,000 in Q4-25; Rep. Mike Rogers; Speaker Johnson's committee). No pro-Israel PAC money or super PAC support found.

money2.note: Katie Britt's campaign committee gave $6,000 (Q4 2025, ADN). 1819 News reported a $10,000 Britt donation (headline only, not opened).

note.t: As a first-time federal candidate he must file a House candidate financial disclosure. disclosures-clerk.house.gov could not be searched, and Quiver's page showed no data. His Alabama Ethics Commission statement of economic interests was not reviewed.

Lives in Enterprise (Coffee County), which is in AL-02 under the 2023 map. He switched from AL-01 to AL-02 for that reason and won Coffee County with over 60% in the special primary. He represents Coffee County's HD-91 since 2018; total years of residence not documented.

checks.legal: CourtListener/Justia blocked, Alacourt paywalled, Alabama Ethics Commission not searched. Wikipedia and Ballotpedia list no legal matters. A dedicated news search was not run because the search budget ran out.
checks.foreign: FARA blocked; House candidate disclosure and Alabama Ethics Commission statement not reachable. No foreign ties surfaced in sources reviewed.
checks.claims: Campaign site rhettforalabama.com could not be opened. Sample = every checkable claim in his campaign-launch statement (ADN/NBC 15/APR, Aug 2025), plus record claims in Reflector's Aug 11, 2026 report, plus his two most-covered ads (first AL-2 ad, Jul 14, 2026; 'Alabama Common Sense', Apr 21, 2026). 8 rated: 6 true, 1 partly, 1 unverifiable. The 2026 death-penalty-law claim was not rated (vote not opened).
checks.democracy: Never in Congress. No search for statements on 2020/2024 results was completed.

recordx.note: Not a member of Congress. FEC committee page shows only the Statement of Organization in the filings table (loads by script), so RFAI status was not determined. Disclosure timeliness unknown.

research_notes: Special primary (Aug 11, 2026, winner-take-all): about 50% (Reflector unofficial: 15,468 votes at 62% counted) over Hampton Harris (~20%) and David Matthews (~18%). Endorsements: Trump (June 2026), Sen. Katie Britt (from his 2025 launch), Speaker Ledbetter and 31 House Republicans (Sep 2025), NRCC. Cash on hand fell from >$775K at end of 2025 (ADN) to $187,718 at Jul 22, 2026 (FEC), reflecting primary spending in both AL-01 and AL-02. The Reflector (Aug 11, 2026) describes the gas-tax vote as a '2018 vote'; Rebuild Alabama passed in March 2019, after he took office in Nov 2018. The DCCC's attack lines (gas tax, Medicaid cuts, Iran war) are party opposition claims and are reported only as such. The web-search budget ran out partway through.
